overview: Gunadule, also called Guna, Kuna or Tule, communities live in Colombia and Panama. This imported outline lies around Colombian Urabá and Darién, rather than covering the whole people or a later Panamanian comarca. Its 1492-1500 dates are map coverage. The relationship between early colonial populations and today’s Gunadule requires more care than a single colored polygon can convey.

periods.title: An uncertain early identification
periods.summary: The imported label predates clear Gunadule names in the cited Spanish records; earlier identity remains debated.

periods.title: Networks and community continuity
periods.summary: From approximately 1610, colonial records document Gunadule names and resistance; later communities continued on both sides of the modern border.

periods.title: Documenting language and knowledge
periods.summary: A community self-assessment examined language use and learning in Colombian Tule households.

items.text: ICANH traces Gunadule names in Spanish chronicles to around 1610, including Tunacunas, Cunacunas and Darienes. Communities defended their independence and sometimes allied with English and French privateers against Spanish power. Such alliances were part of regional politics, rather than evidence that everyone followed one distant ruler.

At the Darién museum, Gunadule and Emberá voices describe sacred histories carried by community authorities and passed to children. Their accounts connect living communities to the landscape. ICANH also notes uncertainty about the identity of earlier inhabitants, presenting distinct kinds of evidence side by side.

Colombian Gunadule communities include Caimán Nuevo in Antioquia and Arquía in Chocó. Panamanian communities have different regional arrangements. These places belong to a connected people, but their local authorities and territorial histories should not be flattened into one modern province.

The Colombian self-assessment describes extended households in which married daughters could remain with their parents while husbands joined their wives’ families. It also records riverside houses with palm roofs, cane or bamboo walls and earth floors. This describes a particular documented household pattern, not every family’s home.

The same study describes the community congress as a central place for decisions. Chiefs, spokespeople, community officers and specialists in plants and therapeutic songs had recognized roles. Public discussion linked practical government with the knowledge held by different members of the community.

Artesanías de Colombia describes farming and fishing as historical foundations of Gunadule subsistence. Textile work also earns money for households in Caimán Nuevo and Arquía. Making a beautiful blouse can therefore connect artistic knowledge with buying the other things a family needs.

sections.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write

items.text: The Gold Museum collection includes a recent Gunadule blouse decorated with a geometric mola, catalogue A00660. Its recorded dimensions are 31.5 by 41 centimeters. The design is made from layers of cloth joined with needle and thread, a compact object holding a great deal of patient work.

Mola makers use both geometric and recognizable figurative designs. Artesanías de Colombia identifies these as different categories of work. The precision comes from applying cloth to cloth: a vivid pattern depends on tiny stitches as much as on bold colors.

In the 2016 study of protective molas, participants connect designs with caring for girls, women, the community and the Earth. These are spiritual meanings explained by the people who preserve them. A pattern may carry responsibilities and stories as well as decoration.

The study describes a sagla, a community authority, drawing protective mola designs with a notebook, pencil and ruler. Designs remembered through teaching become new drawings. This documented visual practice is distinct from writing spoken sentences with an alphabet.

A short alphabetic sample appears as a heading in the 2016 article: “Anmala gunadulemala bia daniggi”, translated alongside it as “Where do we Gunadule come from?” It is a modern published witness to the language, separate from the patterned visual language of molas.

The museum’s learning activity explains that Guna girls in Colombian Urabá and Panama’s Caribbean communities learn to sew mola designs for their blouses. Lessons can take place through watching and practicing. The cloth becomes something to wear and something through which skill passes between generations.

The 2009 Colombian language assessment found that families were the main setting for learning Tule. It also discussed a curriculum designed with community authorities and knowledgeable elders, alongside parents’ desire for Spanish and mathematics. Education involved choosing how several kinds of knowledge could fit together.

ending.text: The map cutoff is not the end of the Gunadule. Communities persist in Colombia and Panama, with their own authorities, language teaching and artistic knowledge. This Colombian outline is not a substitute for the separate histories of Panamanian comarcas.
